newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: RUGBY UNION-FIVE NATIONS PEACE DEAL REVEALS BONUS CLAUSE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FIVE NATIONS PEACE DEAL REVEALS BONUS CLAUSE.

text.p: England and their Five Nations championship rivals now have extra incentives to perform on the field as a result of the peace plan which has assured the tournament's survival well into the 21st century.

Details of the deal which saved England from expulsion following their refusal to back down in a dispute over television revenue were announced by the Five Nations Committee on Monday and included an unprecedented performance-related clause.
Ninety per cent of revenue raised from broadcast rights will be split equally, but five per cent will be allocated according to each country's record in the tournament.

Half the latter amount will go to the winners, 1.5 percent to the runners-up and 1 percent to the third-placed nation. Although no official figure is being divulged, the winning union could receive a bonus approaching 1 million pounds ($1.56 million).

Five per cent will be also be split according to the number of clubs affiliated to each union, English rugby's frequent bone of contention and one of the reasons behind the decision to bypass normal practice and sell rights to their matches to satellite broadcasters BSkyB.

That contract remains in place for five years, but England have been warned all future deals must be done jointly and told to pay a so-far unspecified sum into a central `pot' from the revenue generated each year by Twickenham Five Nations games.
The committee have also insisted on a fair balance between matches shown on terrestrial channels compared with cable or satellite, leaving all sides in the dispute relatively happy.
Vernon Pugh, chairman of the Five Nations TV committee commented: "We have taken sensible, commercial decisions. We have a duty to the public. Most, if not everybody, will be satisfied."

The new broadcasting agreement also includes France, who have previously negotiated their own television deals for language reasons. The French Rugby Federation have signed the accord, but it has yet to be ratified by their full committee.

Tom Kiernan, the Five Nations committee chairman, claimed rugby was now "well placed to grow and prosper into the new millennium" and it seems England, despite the concessions they have made, now have the financial muscle to sort out the dispute between their union and the leading clubs.

England's income from television alone is set to rise from next season to 13 million pounds ($20.27 million) from 2.5 million pounds ($3.90 million), and they can now afford to pay the 4.2 million pounds ($6.55 million) per year they promised to the clubs before the BSkyB deal was jeopardised.
Cliff Brittle, chairman of the Rugby Football Union (RFU) executive committee, rejected suggestions England had been bullied into an agreement.
"There are no losers. There have been major concessions by both parties. It is a fair agreement. We are united again.
"By using intelligence and common sense we have brought peace with the Five Nations. Now let the same criteria bring peace between our union and our clubs."

Any union wishing to withdraw from the tournament must now give five years notice, starting no earlier than the end of June 2002, and a unanimous vote is required on all future format and financial issues.
Kiernan commented: "We are simply delighted and relieved the Five Nations has been restored. Rugby people will be overjoyed."
